title: Changes in Hospital Income, Use, and Quality Associated With Private Equity Acquisition
author: Joseph D. Bruch · Suhas Gondi · Zirui Song

dom.t: Healthcare ownership: Financial gains do not prove patient benefit

st.t: Healthcare ownership: Financial gains do not prove patient benefit
st.an: The study supports the cluster’s proposition by associating private-equity acquisition with higher hospital income and charges while finding quality improvements only on some measures, no significant change on another, and deterioration in a non-HCA subgroup. Its observational framing and subgroup heterogeneity reinforce the distinction between financial gains and demonstrated patient benefit.
qs: **CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE:** Hospitals acquired by private equity were associated with larger increases in net income, charges, charge to cost ratios, and case mix index as well as with improvement in some quality measures after acquisition relative to nonacquired controls.

Non-HCA hospitals showed a decrease in the aggregate heart failure score (-3.3%; 95% CI, -5.3% to -1.3%; P = .01) and no statistically significant changes in the aggregate score for acute myocardial infarction (2.4%; 95% CI, -0.7% to 5.4%; P > .99) or pneumonia (0.2%; 95% CI, -1.4% to 1.7%; P > .99).

mo.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: Study evaluates private equity acquisition effects
kp.d: The cohort study compared 204 hospitals acquired by private equity firms from 2005 to 2017 with 532 matched nonacquired hospitals. Using a difference-in-differences design, it evaluated income, use, and aggregate quality changes through 3 years after acquisition, with covariate and multiple-testing adjustments.
qs: This cohort study identified 204 hospitals acquired by private equity firms from 2005 to 2017 and 532 matched hospitals not acquired by private equity.

Using a difference-in-differences design, this study evaluated changes in net income, charges, charge to cost ratios, case mix index (a measure of reported illness burden), share of discharges for patients with Medicare or Medicaid coverage, discharges per year, and aggregate hospital quality measures associated with private equity acquisition through 3 years after acquisition, adjusted for case mix, hospital beds, calendar year, and adjustment for multiple hypothesis testing.

kp.k: Acquired hospitals increased income and charges
kp.d: Relative to controls, private equity-acquired hospitals had a mean annual net-income increase of $2,302,391, a $407 increase in total charge per inpatient day, and increases of 0.61 and 0.31 in emergency-department and total charge-to-cost ratios, respectively. Each reported difference was statistically significant after the study's adjustments.
qs: Relative to 532 control hospitals, the 204 private equity-acquired hospitals showed a mean increase of $2 302 391 (95% CI, $956 660-$3 648 123; P = .009) in annual net income, an increase of $407 (95% CI, $296-$518; P < .001) in total charge per inpatient day, an increase of 0.61 (95% CI, 0. 48-0.73; P < .001) in emergency department charge to cost ratio, an increase of 0.31 (95% CI, 0.26-0.37; P < .001) in total charge to cost ratio

kp.k: Case mix rose while Medicare share declined
kp.d: Acquired hospitals experienced a 0.02 relative increase in case mix index and a 0.96% relative decrease in Medicare's share of discharges. Medicaid's discharge share and total annual discharges did not change differentially in a statistically significant manner.
qs: an increase of 0.02 (95% CI, 0.01-0.02; P = .007) in case mix index, and a decrease of 0.96% (95% CI, 0.46%-1.45%; P = .002) in share of Medicare discharges.

Medicaid's share of discharges (-0.16%; 95% CI, -0.86% to 0.53%; P > .99) and total hospital discharges (98; 95% CI, -54 to 250; P > .99) did not change differentially in a statistically significant manner.

kp.d: Relative to controls, acquired hospitals' aggregate quality scores increased by 3.3% for acute myocardial infarction and 2.9% for pneumonia. The 1.3% estimated change in the aggregate heart-failure score was not statistically significant.
qs: The aggregate quality score for acute myocardial infarction increased by 3.3% (95% CI, 1.6%-5.0%; P = .002), and the aggregate score for pneumonia increased by 2.9% (95% CI, 1.8%-3.9%; P < .001) in private equity-acquired hospitals relative to controls.
The aggregate score for heart failure (1.3%; 95% CI, -0.2% to 2.7%; P = .92) did not differentially change in a statistically significant manner.

kp.k: Results differed between HCA and non-HCA hospitals
kp.d: HCA hospitals showed findings similar to the overall sample, but non-HCA hospitals had fewer statistically significant changes: a higher emergency-department charge-to-cost ratio, a lower Medicare discharge share, and a lower aggregate heart-failure quality score. Their myocardial-infarction and pneumonia scores did not change significantly.
qs: In subgroup analyses, HCA hospitals showed similar findings to the entire sample.

Among non-HCA hospitals, the only statistically significant relative changes were the increase in the emergency department charge to cost ratio (0.30; 95% CI, 0.12-0.48; P = .02) and the decrease in Medicare's share (-1.15%; 95% CI, -1.88% to -0.43%; P = . 02).

Non-HCA hospitals showed a decrease in the aggregate heart failure score (-3.3%; 95% CI, -5.3% to -1.3%; P = .01) and no statistically significant changes in the aggregate score for acute myocardial infarction (2.4%; 95% CI, -0.7% to 5.4%; P > .99) or pneumonia (0.2%; 95% CI, -1.4% to 1.7%; P > .99).

kp.k: Conclusions describe associations rather than causation
kp.d: The authors conclude that acquisition was associated with larger increases in net income, charges, charge-to-cost ratios, and reported case mix, alongside improvements in some quality measures. They qualify the overall pattern by emphasizing heterogeneity between HCA and non-HCA hospitals.
qs: Hospitals acquired by private equity were associated with larger increases in net income, charges, charge to cost ratios, and case mix index as well as with improvement in some quality measures after acquisition relative to nonacquired controls.
Heterogeneity in some findings was observed between HCA and non-HCA hospitals.

pts.k: Bruch, Gondi and Song report associations between private equity acquisition and changes in hospital finances, use and selected quality measures. This cross-domain source makes no claims about AI or legal services.
pts.d: Relative to matched nonacquired hospitals, acquired hospitals showed increases in annual net income ($2,302,391), total charges per inpatient day ($407), emergency department charge-to-cost ratio (0.61), total charge-to-cost ratio (0.31), and case mix index (0.02), alongside a reduction in Medicare's share of discharges (reported as 0.96%). Medicaid's share and total discharges did not change differentially in a statistically significant manner. Aggregate quality scores improved for acute myocardial infarction (reported as 3.3%) and pneumonia (2.9%), but not significantly for heart failure. These are retrospective findings expressed as associations, not predictions or assertions that acquisition caused the changes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors base their findings on a matched observational cohort study using difference-in-differences analysis.
pts.d: The study compared 204 hospitals acquired by private equity with 532 matched hospitals not acquired by private equity. It examined eight income and use measures and three aggregate quality measures, adjusting for case mix, hospital beds and calendar year, with adjustment for multiple hypothesis testing. Results include confidence intervals and P values; for example, the estimated annual net-income increase was $2,302,391 (95% CI, $956,660–$3,648,123; P = .009). Separate analyses compared HCA and non-HCA acquired hospitals with matched controls.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern acquisitions from 2005–2017 and changes through three years after acquisition, with important differences between HCA and non-HCA hospitals.
pts.d: The 2020 paper does not offer a forecast beyond the observation window. Its estimates describe adjusted changes relative to matched controls, rather than absolute changes attributable solely to ownership. HCA findings resembled the overall sample. Among non-HCA hospitals, the only statistically significant income/use changes were a higher emergency department charge-to-cost ratio and a lower Medicare discharge share. Non-HCA hospitals also had a statistically significant decline in the aggregate heart failure quality score, with no significant changes in the other two quality scores. The overall quality findings therefore do not apply uniformly across the subgroups.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The measured changes concern acquired hospitals, their payer mix and condition-specific aggregate quality, with distinct findings for HCA and non-HCA institutions.
pts.d: At the hospital level, acquisition was associated with increased income and charges in the overall sample. Medicare patients accounted for a smaller share of discharges, while Medicaid's share did not change significantly. This is a finding about discharge composition, not a demonstrated reduction in access. Quality measures concerned care for acute myocardial infarction, pneumonia and heart failure; the abstract does not establish changes in individual patient outcomes or out-of-pocket spending. For non-HCA hospitals, the emergency department charge-to-cost ratio rose by 0.30, Medicare's discharge share fell by a reported 1.15%, and the aggregate heart failure score fell by 3.3%.
